chapter_theme: Songs at Thiruvannamalai (திருவருணை, 4 of 6): the poet confesses infatuation with women, the body's birth, decay and corpse, and the hour of Death, and asks for Murugan's feet, for release and for a place among his devotees; one song is a love-lament in a girl's voice and one a chant of the five syllables joined to the name of Arunachala; the praise returns to the hill of fire, the tower, Murugan as Siva's teacher and as the saint who defeated the Jains.
structure_note: Courtesan and love songs (414, 415, 417, 418, 424), with 420 and 427 keeping the feet in mind within the embrace; the course of a life from womb to pyre (416, 423) and the body as carrion (422); Death's coming (426); union with Siva (421); a girl's love-lament (413); praise with a short plea (419); and a mantra song (425).

413.reading: In a girl's voice: in the groves the cruel horn of Kama sounds, the wind presses, his five flower arrows strike her on her bed, and one night seems as long as an age; she asks Murugan, lest her mind be ruined, to come and give her his kadamba garland where the bees roam. The praise names him the guru whom Siva with serpent, crescent, river and gems in his hair thought on, the one with six faces, kura flowers, the peacock, the hunter girl and Lakshmi on his chest, whose vel made Meru, Sura and the sea afraid, standing in the holy street of Arunapuri.
413.nuance: ஊரும் உலகும் பழைய பேருகம் விளைந்ததென ஓரிரவு: a single night of separation feels like an aeon, the lover's sense of time. The plea for the god's garland is the conventional request of the love-sick girl.

414.reading: The poet asks Murugan to come on the peacock so that he does not wander without virtue, ruined by women's voices skilled in song and their dark tied hair. The praise names him the warrior whom the deceitful asuras feared, Kumaresa at Sonagiri, the one who spoke a single word into the ear of the First One, and the younger brother of the elephant-faced god.
414.nuance: ஆதியர் காது ஒருச்சொல் அருள்வோனே: the teaching whispered into Siva's ear, here 'one word' without naming Om.

415.reading: The poet tells how women show off combed hair, darting eyes and coral mouths, speak sweetly and loosen their garments, and how he, cruel one, spent his wealth, youth, learning and mind on them until the world mocked him as an outcast and his understanding was ruined by the senses; he asks whether Murugan, master of the common stance at Arunai, will not think to keep his servant under his gaze. The praise names him the one who taught Siva the one hard-to-know thing, the young one born as six children in the Saravana pool where the heavenly women nursed him, the vel that made the seas cry out, and the one who guarded the millet and embraced the hunter girl.
415.nuance: பொருள் இளமை கலை மனமும் ஏகப் போக்கிய புலையன் இவன்: the loss is itemised, wealth, youth, learning and mind, and the world's verdict 'outcast' is quoted. அறுசிறுவர் ஒருவுடலமாகித் தோற்றிய: the six infants of the Saravana pool who became one body.

416.reading: The poet runs through a life, infant, youth in passion, householder loving his home, wanderer, bent old man, the life gone and the body dust with the firewood, and says he never knew this; he asks whether, beyond the six supports of the body and with a body trained in many yogas, he will now reach the undying home of the Lord of deathless knowledge. The praise is Murugan's battle: the seven seas, Meru, Brahma and the Veda and the sun put to flight, the old serpent and the underworld shaken, the mountain split in two, and Indra and the gods given back their city, at Arunai.
416.nuance: The first lines are a life in one breath, as in 9 and 110. பழய சடாதாரம் ... நிராதர: the six adharas of the yogic body and the supportless state beyond them; the plea moves from impermanence to yoga, but the words of the third and fourth lines are hard to divide.

417.reading: The poet confesses that, sunk in infatuation with women wearing ketaki flowers, with petty thoughts, no learning by listening, and deeds of fate bent on his ruin, he has become a great sinner wandering the earth in vain; he asks Murugan to come on the peacock with the vel to rule him and grant release. The praise names him the child who uprooted Taraka, destroyer of justice, so the gods returned to their homes, Vishnu's nephew, the one who dwells in the northern tower of Sonagiri, the hill that rose as fire and light, and the one who took up the sword against the asuras.
417.nuance: கேள்வியதிலாது, ஊழ்வினையினால்: lack of learning and fate are named together as causes, but the plea does not excuse him; he still calls himself பாதகன். சோதி அனலா உதித்த சோணகிரி: the hill as the light that rose as fire.

418.reading: The poet asks not to wander with women on whose breasts and spear-like eyes he dwells, and to be given the feet that shine as his home. The praise names Murugan the one who ran round the sea-girt land on the peacock and the lord praised by the Chola land on the hill of hot light.
418.nuance: ஊராக திகழ் பாதம்: the feet as a town to live in. நீடாழி சுழல் தேசம் வலமாக நீடோடி: circling the world on the peacock, as in 398.

419.reading: The praise names Murugan the guru of Siva, who flayed the elephant and burned the three cities, and asks him, who pierced the golden mountain and trampled the other hill to ash, to come daily on the blue peacock to the minds of those who sing the kadamba with devotion. It names him the hero who embraces the hunter girl on his twelve shoulders, the Sivavel known in the minds of devotees, and the one who broke the gods' prison at Arunai.
419.nuance: The plea is not for the poet himself but for all who sing with devotion (நீபமலர் பத்தி மெத்த ஓதுமவர் சித்தம்): Murugan is asked to come into their minds.

420.reading: The poet describes a sulking woman with kumkum on her bow brow and angry eyes, at whose flower feet he bows until her bangles jingle and love returns, and their union, and asks whether even in that union he would forget Murugan's golden feet in his heart. The praise names Siva, three-eyed and compassionate, who dances beside the mountain's daughter, as the giver of Murugan, the hero who embraced the hunter girl, the one who fought the asuras in the sea, and the lord at Arunagiri who ends the fears of devotees.
420.nuance: புணரினும் நிற் பொற்பதங்கள் நெஞ்சினுள் மறவேனோ: the question means he will not forget; the feet are held in the very act the other songs flee. The lovers' quarrel (புலவி) and the bowing at her feet are classical akam, told as the poet's own.

421.reading: The poet asks that, enjoying union with Siva's consort and with his hunger stilled by the nectar of Siva-knowledge, the two becoming one form and all the worlds enjoyed, he may play at the Lord's side while Vishnu, Brahma and the gods say 'this is the one' and the Vedas chant, and that Murugan grant this with his vel and peacock. The praise names him the one who threw the fiery vel so that the asuras' heads and the seven seas were dust, the chest that embraced the hunter girl, and the lord of the great fire hill, asked to end the poet's poverty and disease.
421.nuance: சிவஞான அமுதே பசியாறி, இருவோர் ஒரு ரூபமதாய்: hunger stilled by knowledge and two becoming one form describe union with Siva, an unusually high plea. The ending asks for the end of poverty (மிடி) as well. A letter is lost in line 3, and who the 'two' are is not certain.

422.reading: The poet sees his body as what dogs, jackals, vultures, kites, demons and worms feed on gladly, a mire of filth and bones caught between the nets of birth and death, taking more forms than the sand of the sky could count; he asks that, calling his body and life Murugan's due, he be taken into service and joined to the devotees, and asks whether Murugan will not think of him today. The praise is a battle in drum syllables, the vel that sets the worlds rejoicing while Vishnu and Brahma serve and sing, and Murugan as the lord whom the Sankara of Arunagiri, with Gauri at his side and Ganga, worships.
422.nuance: செனனவலை மரணவலை ரண்டும் முன்பின் தொடர்ந்து: birth and death as two nets, one before and one behind. The remedy is not solitary but the company of devotees (அன்பரோடே கலவி நலம் மருவி), and கடன் எனது உடலுயிரும் makes body and life a debt owed to the Lord.

423.reading: The poet traces his making from seed and blood in the womb, growing like a pill, the belly swelling and the body's heat rising until birth in the tenth month, then crying, nursing, crawling, toddling, learning only empty knowledge and sinking into infatuation with peacock-like women, and asks whether he will waste away in birth like this. The praise names Vishnu who destroyed the southern rakshasas and gave a kingdom to the one who came to him, the guru Siva who burned the three cities, Uma who woke all the worlds as his mother, the vel that set the seas on fire, and the coral-hued hunter girl, at Arunai.
423.nuance: கற்று வெற்றறிவு பெற்று: learning itself is listed among the stages that lead nowhere. The giving of a kingdom to a southern suppliant after the rakshasas' fall points to Vibhishana, though the name is garbled.

424.reading: The poet quotes his own flattery of women, breasts like pots and an elephant's brow, teeth like pearls, lips sweeter than fruit, hair like clouds, Lakshmi of the lotus, young vanji twig, peacock, and calls himself the dull-witted fool who coaxes, pleads and daily worships their feet; he asks when he will reach Murugan's feet. The praise names Siva who drank the poison, who took the form of the fierce Sarabha bird to stop the man-lion that tore Hiranya with its claws, and Uma his chaste consort as Murugan's mother, and Murugan as the old man who roamed the hunters' millet field, on the peacock at Arunapuri.
424.nuance: The flattery is given as direct speech, so the poet's folly is shown, not described: he worships the women's feet (தினமவர் தாடொழு) where he should worship Murugan's. வெஞ்சச் சிம்புள் சொருபமதானவர்: Siva as the Sarabha subduing Narasimha. திரிகிழவா: Murugan's disguise as an old man to court Valli.

425.reading: The song chants 'Jaya jaya Arunadri' with the five syllables of Siva in each of their rotations, then asks whether, fixing his eyes on Arunadri and melting at 'Hara Hara Saranadri', the poet will drink the sea-nectar of the Siva-word at the holy feet. The praise names Murugan the vel that burned the asuras, the one who spoke into the two ears of the red Siva-light whose head and feet the two seekers could not find, the golden guru who showed the dance in the space of light that powders the two deeds, and the lord who delights in Arunadri, the hill of Siva.
425.nuance: The opening rotates the five letters in order, சிவயநம, மசிவயந, நமசிவய, யநமசிவ, வயநமசி, each joined to அருணாத்திரி, so the mantra and the hill are one chant. திருமுடி அடி ... இருவர்க்கு அடிதலை தெரியாப்படி: Brahma and Vishnu failing to find the ends of the column of light is the story of Arunachala, and Murugan is the one who taught that light.

426.reading: The poet pictures the lone Death on his buffalo, dark as a mass of night with fiery eyes and horns like black serpents, throwing the noose while he sits in anxious thought and his kin and sons weep at the hour ripe for death; he asks Murugan to come then with his lotus faces, smile, long eyes, earrings, vel and dancing peacock, and grant him a boon. The praise names him the one who drank the milk of the mountain's daughter, who taught the Agama to the bowing lords, who split Sura, who set the Jains gathered at Koodal kicking on the stakes, son of Ganga, easy to reach for devotees, at the great tower of Arunai.
426.nuance: The plea is the familiar one of 8 and 46, but the picture of Murugan coming is unusually full, face, smile, ornaments and anklets, as if the sight itself were the rescue. இளமுலையின் செழும்பால் குடுத்து and அமணர் ... கூடலில் ... கழுவில்: the milk of Uma and the impaled Jains of Madurai are Sambandar's story, here given to Murugan.

427.reading: The poet lists women's charms, voices like cuckoo, peacock, dove, parrot and bee, mountainous breasts, spear eyes, crescent brow, dark hair, bright teeth, moon face and swan gait, and seems to say that even if he sports with such women in bed he will not let go of Murugan's anklet-sounding lotus feet, the cock banner and his form beyond painting. The praise is a battle in drum syllables, the vel that made the seven seas dust, Siva who gives the white ash to end the poet's sorrow, Uma who bore 'us' and bore Murugan, and Valli's lover who ends the poet's two deeds and malas, at the hill of fire.
427.nuance: If அன்தகையேனே is read 'I will not be held back from', the song makes the same vow as 420, keeping the feet in mind in the embrace. அடியேன் துயர் தீர்ந்திட வெண்தழல் மாபொடி அருள்வோர்: Siva's gift of holy ash for the poet's sorrow. Line 16 is corrupt.

links.note: Both speak for a girl sick with love for Murugan, tormented by Kama's five flower arrows, and ask him to come with his garland; 101 is spoken for her, 413 by her, and adds that one night feels like an age.
Both run a life from the embryo in the womb through birth, nursing and crawling to desire for women. 9 ends in disease; 423 counts learning among the stages, calling it empty knowledge.

Tirumular lists the rotations of the five-letter mantra in order from SI: சிவயநம, மசிவயந, நமசிவய, யநமசிவ, வயநமசி. 425 chants the same rotations in the same order, each joined to the name of Arunachala, making a teaching of the mantra into a hymn to the hill.

Both make Murugan the Tamil saint who sent the Jains of Madurai to the stakes. 104 adds Pugali and the cure of the king's fever; 426 adds the milk the mountain's daughter gave, the other mark of Sambandar's story.

Both show vultures tearing at the body. The Naladiyar's stinking cart is shown to men who praise sandal and garlands; 422 sees the poet's own body as the feast of dogs, jackals, vultures and worms, and turns from it to the company of devotees.

The Kural's woman says the long nights now passing are crueller than the cruel man himself (கொடியார் கொடுமையின் தாம்கொடிய இந்நாள் நெடிய கழியும் இரா). 413's girl, struck by Kama's five flower arrows on her bed, says one night has come on like an old aeon (பழைய பேருகம் விளைந்ததென ஓரிரவு). Both make the lengthened night, not the absent lover, the torment of separation.

414 names Murugan only as the one who spoke a single word into the First One's ear (ஆதியர் காது ஒருச்சொல் அருள்வோனே). 176 tells the same act and names the word: the secret of the pranava spoken into Siva's golden ear (பொற்செவியுட் பிரணவ ரகசியம்). The fuller song supplies what 414's 'one word' is.

The Naladiyar says those who think the love of a worthless woman their own, while she licks like a wild cow and takes the wealth from their hands, will be laughed at by many (பலரால் நகை). 415 confesses the same end from inside: wealth, youth, learning and mind spent on such women (பொருள் இளமை கலை மனமும் ஏகப் போக்கிய), until the world reviles him as an outcast (புலையன் இவன் என உலகம் ஏச). The quatrain's warning is the song's confession.

The Tirumanthiram says people see the times called child, youth and old man pass and still do not understand (பாலன் இளையன் விருத்தன் ... கண்டும் அறிகிலார்). 416 runs the same stages, infant, youth, householder, bent old man, to the body made dust with the firewood, and says of itself that it never knew this (மறியாதாய்). Both turn from the passing of ages to the feet or home that does not pass.

The Kural says nothing is stronger than fate: devise another way and it is there first (ஊழிற் பெருவலி யாவுள). 417 names fate as a cause of its ruin, deeds of fate bent on harm (ஊழ்வினையினால் மிகுத்த கேடுறுகவே நினைக்கும் வினை), yet asks Murugan to come with the vel to rule him and grant release (வீடுதவி ஆள). On the reading that the plea expects grace to override what fate decreed, the song sets a limit to the Kural's 'no greater strength'.

The Tirumanthiram orders it: praise and sing the Pure One's form, turn back the five senses, then pour the Lord into the heart (போற்றிசைத்து ... நாதனை ஊற்றுக உள்ளத்து). 419 asks Murugan to come daily on the peacock into the minds of those who sing the kadamba with full devotion (நீபமலர் பத்தி மெத்த ஓதுமவர் சித்தம்). In both, singing praise is the way the Lord comes to dwell in the heart.

The Kural names quarrelling, making up and union as the fruits of those who love (ஊடல் உணர்தல் புணர்தல் இவைகாமம் கூடியார் பெற்ற பயன்). 420 tells exactly that course, the sulk (புலவி மிகுத்திட்டு), bowing at her flower feet until love returns (அநுராகம்), and union, then asks whether even in union he would forget the golden feet (புணரினும் நிற் பொற்பதங்கள் நெஞ்சினுள் மறவேனோ). The song keeps the Kural's sequence but holds the feet above its fruit.

The Tirumanthiram describes the one made one with the Supreme (பரத்துடன் ஏகமாய்), stilled like clear water after waves, who has fully tasted the rare nectar (ஆரமுது ஒக்க உணர்ந்துளோன்). 421 asks for the same end in a devotee's words: hunger stilled by the nectar of Siva-knowledge (சிவஞான அமுதே பசியாறி) and the two becoming one form (இருவோர் ஒரு ரூபமதாய்). Union and nectar go together in both.

The Tirumanthiram's poet entered the Lord's city by going with the devotees of the Lord's devotees (உடையான் அடியார் அடியாருடன் போய்). 422, after seeing his body as carrion between the nets of birth and death, asks for a share with the loving servants (அன்புறும் தொண்டர் பங்குறுக) and to delight in union with the devotees (அன்பரோடே கலவி நலம் மருவி). Both reach the Lord in company, not alone.

The Tirumanthiram says the form grows ten bright months, comes into the world in its season, and grows mingled with maya (ஒண்டிங்கள் பத்திற் ... மருவி வளர்ந்திடு மாயையினாலே). 423 traces the same: seed and blood in the womb, birth in the tenth month (மதி சொற்ற பத்தின்), then growth into empty learning and bathing in infatuation (மயலிற் குளித்து). The song fills in the life the verse compresses.

The Naladiyar mocks the untaught petty men who babble that smiles are jasmine buds and pearls (முல்லை முகைமுறுவல் முத்தென்று இவைபிதற்றும் கல்லாப்புன் மாக்கள்), having seen the teeth in the burning ground. 424 quotes such flattery in its own mouth, teeth like rows of pearls (பந்தித் தரளம்), lips sweeter than fruit, and names the speaker a dull-witted fool (மந்தப் புந்திக் கசடன்). The quatrain's mocked praiser is the poet's self-portrait.

420 asks whether even in union he would forget the golden feet in his heart (புணரினும் நிற் பொற்பதங்கள் நெஞ்சினுள் மறவேனோ). 427, after a long list of women's charms, seems to make the same vow, that even sporting with them in bed (அமளியின் ஆடினும்) he will keep to the lotus feet with their anklets (பூங்கமலம் சரண்). On that reading the two songs hold the feet in mind within the embrace, where most of the book flees it.

source_issues: Song 414: one corrupt character in கி஡ணயி (line 6); here ஡ண stands for ரி, so கிரியில் (Sonagiri), not ரீ as in songs 12 and 88.
Song 418: நீடோ டி (line 6) has a stray space inside the vowel sign; read நீடோடி.
Song 421: line 3 reads ஒ ரு பமதாய் with a letter lost; probably ஒரு ரூபமதாய் ('one form').
Song 425: line 3 ends தி முலா after the beat marks, an unflagged fragment that fits neither the mantra rotation nor the following line.
Song 426: line 8 begins with four dots (....) instead of six; harmless.
Song 427: line 16 begins with the unflagged garble திநச்முடுக; the sense (the seven seas turned to dust) survives.
